messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Piezo Energy Harvester: Sinusoidal current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$, capacitance $C_p$, leakage $R_{leak}=20 \text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   Load: $R_L$ varies (150 k$\Omega$ to 2200 k$\Omega$).
    *   Target: Output $V_{out}$ from 1.8 V to 3.6 V, ripple $\le 50 \text{ mV}$, startup $\le 0.4 \text{ s}$, settled mean change $\le 0.02 \text{ V}$.
    *   Constraints: Max 16 components, max 4 switches, max 2 SYNC controllers.
    *   Reference Design (FBR): Failed on $V_{out\_min}$ (S2, S4), $V_{out\_max}$ (S3), ripple (S3), startup (S2, S4), and stability (S1, S3, S4, S5).

    *   S1: $I_p=50\mu\text{A}, f=100\text{Hz}, C_p=25\text{nF}, R_L=330\text{k}\Omega \implies V_{oc} \approx 3.18\text{V}$
    *   S2: Heavy load ($R_L=150\text{k}\Omega$) $\implies$ High power consumption, harder to reach $V_{out\_min}$.
    *   S3: Strong excitation, light load ($I_p=100\mu\text{A}, R_L=2200\text{k}\Omega$) $\implies$ Higher energy, risk of $V_{out} > 3.6\text{V}$.
    *   S4: Weak excitation ($I_p=30\mu\text{A}, R_L=1000\text{k}\Omega$) $\implies$ Lower energy, harder to reach $V_{out\_min}$.
    *   S5: Low frequency ($f=80\text{Hz}$) $\implies$ Lower energy density per second.
    *   S6: High temp, $C_p+20\%$ ($C_p=30\text{nF}$).

    *   The FBR is a passive rectifier. It's simple but inefficient due to diode drops and lack of impedance matching.
    *   The voltage range (1.8V to 3.6V) is narrow. $V_{oc}$ is $\sim 3.2\text{V}$. Diode drops ($\sim 0.25\text{V} \times 2 = 0.5\text{V}$) significantly reduce the available voltage for the load.
    *   S3 exceeds 3.6V, so a Zener clamp (DZ33) is likely necessary.
    *   To improve efficiency (especially for S2 and S4), a Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI) or a Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction (SECE) circuit would be better. SSHI flips the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks, increasing the energy extracted per cycle.

    *   **Design 1: SSHI (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor)**
        *   Basic SSHI consists of a piezo, an inductor, a switch, and a rectifier.
        *   The switch closes at the piezo voltage extrema, flipping the charge on $C_p$.
        *   Connectivity: Piezo $\to$ Rectifier $\to$ $C_{out}$. Inductor and Switch are used to invert the voltage.
        *   Actually, a simpler SSHI is: Piezo $\to$ Inductor $L$ $\to$ Switch $S$ (across piezo terminals) $\to$ Rectifier (half or full) $\to$ $C_{out}$.
        *   Let's try a standard SSHI:
            *   Piezo (pzp, pzn)
            *   Inductor $L$ in series with a switch $S$ (connecting pzp to pzn?). No, the switch closes to short the piezo via $L$.
            *   Wait, a standard SSHI is: Piezo $\to$ rectifier $\to$ storage. The switch is in parallel with the piezo (via $L$).
            *   Correct SSHI: Piezo terminals (pzp, pzn). Switch $S$ connects pzp and pzn through inductor $L$. This flips the voltage on $C_p$ at the peaks.
            *   Then a rectifier extracts the energy.
            *   Wait, the most efficient SSHI is usually: Piezo $\to$ Diode $\to$ $C_{out}$. And a switch that connects pzp to pzn via $L$ at the peaks.
            *   Actually, the "Parallel-SSHI" (P-SSHI) puts the inductor/switch in parallel with the piezo.

    *   **Design 2: SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction)**
        *   SECE uses an inductor and a switch to transfer the charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$ at the peaks.
        *   Connectivity: Piezo $\to$ Switch $S$ $\to$ Inductor $L$ $\to$ Diode $D$ $\to$ $C_{out}$.
        *   At the peaks, the switch closes, and the charge $C_p V_p$ is transferred to $L$ and then to $C_{out}$ through $D$.
        *   Since $V_{oc}$ is $3.2\text{V}$ and $V_{out}$ is $1.8\text{V}-3.6\text{V}$, SECE is very effective.

    *   **Design 3: Improved FBR with Zener and larger Capacitor**
        *   To fix S3's overvoltage and S4's undervoltage, we can try a full bridge with a Zener clamp and optimize the storage capacitor. But this is likely just a variant of the reference. Let's go for a more structural change.

    *   *SSHI (Parallel):*
        *   Piezo (pzp, pzn).
        *   Switch $S$ connects pzp and pzn through $L$.
        *   Rectifier (Full bridge) between (pzp, pzn) and (out, 0).
        *   $C_{out}$ from out to 0.
        *   Zener DZ33 from out to 0.
        *   *Pros:* High energy extraction. *Cons:* More components.

    *   *SECE:*
        *   Piezo (pzp, pzn).
        *   Switch $S$ connects pzp to a node `n1`.
        *   Inductor $L$ connects `n1` to a diode $D$.
        *   Diode $D$ connects to `out`.
        *   Wait, SECE requires a switch for the negative peak too, or a bridge.
        *   Dual-switch SECE:
            *   S1 (pzp to n1), S2 (pzn to n2).
            *   L1 (n1 to out), L2 (n2 to out). (Or one L and a bridge).
            *   Better: S1 (pzp to n1), S2 (pzn to n1). L (n1 to n2). D (n2 to out).

    *   *Simplified SSHI (Standard):*
        *   Piezo (pzp, pzn).
        *   Rectifier (Full Bridge) from (pzp, pzn) to (out, 0).
        *   $C_{out}$ (out, 0).
        *   Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo.
        *   Wait, if the switch is in parallel with the piezo, it might short the rectifier.
        *   Correct Parallel-SSHI: The switch and inductor are in parallel with the piezo. The rectifier is also in parallel. To avoid shorting the output through the rectifier, the switch must be carefully placed.
        *   Actually, a common SSHI topology: Piezo $\to$ Full Bridge $\to$ $C_{out}$. The inductor $L$ and switch $S$ are in parallel with the piezo. But when the switch closes, it shorts the piezo. The bridge diodes will block the $C_{out}$ discharge back into the piezo if the bridge is placed correctly.
        *   Let's check: $V_{out} = 2\text{V}$. $V_{pzp} = 3\text{V}$. Switch closes. $V_{pzp}$ drops to $0\text{V}$. $V_{out}$ is still $2\text{V}$. Diodes in bridge: if $V_{pzp} < V_{out} - 0.25\text{V}$, they are reverse biased. So the switch doesn't drain $C_{out}$.

    *   **Proposal 1: SSHI (Full Bridge + Parallel L-S)**
        *   D1: pzp $\to$ out
        *   D2: pzn $\to$ out
        *   D3: 0 $\to$ pzp
        *   D4: 0 $\to$ pzn
        *   L1: pzp $\to$ n1
        *   S1: n1 $\to$ pzn (ctrl: G1)
        *   G1: SYNC, edges: both, ton: 30us (approx $\pi \sqrt{LC_p}$), phase: 0.
        *   C1: out $\to$ 0
        *   DZ1: out $\to$ 0 (Zener clamp)

    *   **Proposal 2: SECE (Simplified)**
        *   S1: pzp $\to$ n1 (ctrl: G1, edges: pos)
        *   S2: pzn $\to$ n1 (ctrl: G2, edges: neg)
        *   L1: n1 $\to$ n2
        *   D1: n2 $\to$ out
        *   C1: out $\to$ 0
        *   DZ1: out $\to$ 0 (Zener clamp)
        *   G1: SYNC, edges: pos
        *   G2: SYNC, edges: neg

    *   **Proposal 3: Half-Bridge SSHI (for simplicity and efficiency)**
        *   D1: pzp $\to$ out
        *   D2: 0 $\to$ pzn (Wait, this is a half-bridge)
        *   Actually, let's go with a "Voltage-Doubler" style SECE or a more robust SSHI.
        *   Let's try a different SSHI:
            *   D1: pzp $\to$ out
            *   D2: pzn $\to$ out
            *   D3: 0 $\to$ pzp
            *   D4: 0 $\to$ pzn
            *   L1: pzp $\to$ n1
            *   S1: n1 $\to$ pzn (ctrl: G1)
            *   C1: out $\to$ 0
            *   S2: out $\to$ pzp (No, that's too complex)
            *   Just add a Zener to the Full Bridge SSHI.

    *   S1: pzp $\to$ n1, ctrl: G1, edges: pos
    *   S2: pzn $\to$ n1, ctrl: G2, edges: neg
    *   L1: n1 $\to$ n2
    *   D1: n2 $\to$ out
    *   C1: out $\to$ 0
    *   DZ1: out $\to$ 0
    *   G1: edges: pos, ton: 30us
    *   G2: edges: neg, ton: 30us
    *   *Rationale:* SECE is generally more efficient than FBR and SSHI for low-frequency piezo harvesting because it extracts the charge regardless of the load, as long as $V_{out}$ is lower than the peak piezo voltage.

    *   Full bridge (DSCH) + L1 + S1 (parallel to piezo) + C1 + DZ1.
    *   L1: pzp $\to$ n1, S1: n1 $\to$ pzn.
    *   G1: edges: both, ton: 30us.
    *   *Rationale:* SSHI increases the available voltage and energy by flipping the capacitance voltage.

    *   Wait, if $V_{oc}$ is $3.2\text{V}$, and we want $V_{out}$ between $1.8\text{V}$ and $3.6\text{V}$, a simple FBR with a Zener might fail because the diode drops ($0.5\text{V}$) bring the peak to $2.7\text{V}$, which is barely above $1.8\text{V}$ once you consider the load.
    *   Let's try a "Charge Pump" or "Voltage Doubler" (Greinacher circuit).
        *   C_fly: pzp $\to$ n1
        *   D1: n1 $\to$ out
        *   D2: pzn $\to$ n1 (No, that's not right)
        *   Standard doubler: C1 (pzp to n1), D1 (n1 to out), D2 (pzn to n1). No.
        *   Correct: C1 (pzp to n1), D1 (n1 to out), D2 (pzn to n1). Still wrong.
        *   Correct: C1 (pzp to n1), D1 (n1 to out), C2 (pzn to n2), D2 (n2 to out). This is just two half-wave rectifiers.

    *   Let's stick to SSHI and SECE. They are the gold standards for piezo.

    *   S1: pzp $\to$ n1, ctrl: G1
    *   S2: pzn $\to$ n1, ctrl: G2
    *   L1: n1 $\to$ n2
    *   D1: n2 $\to$ out
    *   C1: out $\to$ 0
    *   DZ1: out $\to$ 0
    *   G1: edges: pos, ton: 30us, phase: 0.0
    *   G2: edges: neg, ton: 30us, phase: 0.0
    *   S-counts: 2, SYNC-counts: 2, L-counts: 1, D-counts: 2 (D1 and DZ1), C-counts: 1. Total: 6 components.

    *   D1: pzp $\to$ out
    *   D2: pzn $\to$ out
    *   D3: 0 $\to$ pzp
    *   D4: 0 $\to$ pzn
    *   L1: pzp $\to$ n1
    *   S1: n1 $\to$ pzn, ctrl: G1
    *   C1: out $\to$ 0
    *   DZ1: out $\to$ 0
    *   G1: edges: both, ton: 30us, phase: 0.0
    *   D-counts: 5 (including DZ1), L-counts: 1, S-counts: 1, SYNC-counts: 1, C-counts: 1. Total: 8 components.

    *   S1: pzp $\to$ n1, ctrl: G1, edges: pos
    *   L1: n1 $\to$ n2
    *   D1: n2 $\to$ out
    *   S2: pzn $\to$ n3, ctrl: G2, edges: neg
    *   L2: n3 $\to$ n4
    *   D2: n4 $\to$ out
    *   C1: out $\to$ 0
    *   DZ1: out $\to$ 0
    *   (Just another SECE variant)
    *   Let's instead try a **Half-bridge SSHI** as a third option.
    *   D1: pzp $\to$ out
    *   D2: 0 $\to$ pzn
    *   S1: pzp $\to$ n1, ctrl: G1, L1: n1 $\to$ pzn
    *   C1: out $\to$ 0
    *   DZ1: out $\to$ 0
    *   G1: edges: both, ton: 30us.
    *   Actually, a simpler third option: **FBR + Zener + larger storage cap**. No, that's too similar to the reference.
    *   How about a **Synchronous Rectifier** (using switches instead of diodes)?
        *   S1: pzp $\to$ out, ctrl: G1 (pos peak)
        *   S2: pzn $\to$ out, ctrl: G2 (neg peak)
        *   S3: 0 $\to$ pzp, ctrl: G3 (neg peak)
        *   S4: 0 $\to$ pzn, ctrl: G4 (pos peak)
        *   C1: out $\to$ 0
        *   DZ1: out $\to$ 0
        *   G1, G2, G3, G4 are SYNCs. (Wait, limit is 2 SYNCs).
        *   Can G1 control two switches? No, but G1 can be "both".
        *   G1 (both): S1 (pzp to out) and S3 (0 to pzp). (At pos peak, pzp is high, S1 closes. At neg peak, pzp is low, S3 closes).
        *   G2 (both): S2 (pzn to out) and S4 (0 to pzn). (At pos peak, pzn is low, S4 closes. At neg peak, pzn is high, S2 closes).
        *   Wait, this is just a synchronous bridge.

    *   *Refining the Synchronous Bridge (Active Rectifier):*
        *   S1: pzp $\to$ out, ctrl: G1 (edges: pos)
        *   S2: 0 $\to$ pzp, ctrl: G1 (edges: neg)
        *   S3: pzn $\to$ out, ctrl: G2 (edges: neg)
        *   S4: 0 $\to$ pzn, ctrl: G2 (edges: pos)
        *   C1: out $\to$ 0
        *   DZ1: out $\to$ 0
        *   G1: edges: both, ton: 1ms (rectification is not a pulse, it's a half-cycle).
        *   Wait, SYNC `ton` is max 0.001s (1ms). Period is 10ms. So a SYNC cannot be used for a whole half-cycle. It's only for short pulses.
        *   So the active bridge is out.

    *   *Let's go with SECE and SSHI variants.*
        *   Proposal 1: SECE
        *   Proposal 2: SSHI (Full bridge)
        *   Proposal 3: SSHI (Half bridge - simpler, less drop)
            *   D1: pzp $\to$ out
            *   S1: pzp $\to$ n1, ctrl: G1, L1: n1 $\to$ pzn
            *   C1: out $\to$ 0
            *   DZ1: out $\to$ 0
            *   Wait, the half-bridge only harvests half the cycles. Not ideal.
            *   Let's try a **Capacitive-SSHI (CSSHI)** or just another SECE variant.
            *   Let's try SECE with a slightly different diode config. Or just two SECEs.

    *   S1: pzp $\to$ n1, ctrl: G1 (pos)
    *   S2: pzn $\to$ n1, ctrl: G2 (neg)
    *   L1: n1 $\to$ n2
    *   D1: n2 $\to$ out
    *   C1: out $\to$ 0
    *   DZ1: out $\to$ 0
    *   (This is very efficient).

    *   D1: pzp $\to$ out
    *   D2: pzn $\to$ out
    *   D3: 0 $\to$ pzp
    *   D4: 0 $\to$ pzn
    *   L1: pzp $\to$ n1
    *   S1: n1 $\to$ pzn, ctrl: G1 (both)
    *   C1: out $\to$ 0
    *   DZ1: out $\to$ 0
    *   (This increases the energy extracted).

    *   L1: pzp $\to$ n1
    *   S1: n1 $\to$ out, ctrl: G1 (pos)
    *   L2: pzn $\to$ n2
    *   S2: n2 $\to$ out, ctrl: G2 (neg)
    *   C1: out $\to$ 0
    *   DZ1: out $\to$ 0
    *   (Wait, this will discharge `out` back into the piezo).
    *   Needs diodes:
        *   L1: pzp $\to$ n1, S1: n1 $\to$ n2, D1: n2 $\to$ out
        *   L2: pzn $\to$ n3, S2: n3 $\to$ n4, D2: n4 $\to$ out
        *   C1: out $\to$ 0, DZ1: out $\to$ 0.

    *   Actually, let's try a **Zener-clamped FBR with a very large capacitor** as a baseline, just in case. No, that's boring.
    *   Let's go with a **Single-Inductor SECE** and **Parallel-SSHI** and **SECE with an extra storage cap**? No.
    *   Let's try a **synchronous half-wave rectifier with inversion**.
        *   S1: pzp $\to$ out, ctrl: G1 (pos)
        *   S2: pzp $\to$ n1, ctrl: G2 (neg), L1: n1 $\to$ pzn
        *   Wait, this is getting complex.

    *   Let's stick to these two strong candidates and one more:
        *   1: SECE (Single L, dual S)
        *   2: SSHI (Full bridge, single L, single S)
        *   3: SECE (Dual L, dual S) - just to see if the inductor saturation or tuning is better.
        *   Actually, let's try Proposal 3 as a **Half-Bridge SSHI** just to see.
        *   D1: pzp $\to$ out
        *   S1: pzp $\to$ n1, ctrl: G1 (both), L1: n1 $\to$ pzn
        *   C1: out $\to$ 0
        *   DZ1: out $\to$ 0
        *   Wait, if the bridge is a half-bridge, we only get energy from the positive peak. Let's use a full bridge.

    *   Let's refine the SSHI (Full Bridge) to be the most robust.
        *   Rectifier: FBR (4x DSCH)
        *   L-S loop: L1 (pzp to n1), S1 (n1 to pzn)
        *   C_out: 2.2uF
        *   Zener: DZ33 (out to 0)
        *   G1: both, ton: 30us, phase: 0.0

    *   And the SECE:
        *   S1: pzp $\to$ n1 (G1, pos)
        *   S2: pzn $\to$ n1 (G2, neg)
        *   L1: n1 $\to$ n2
